explanation.body: A stronger wind exerts a larger force on the flag and can make it flap with a larger amplitude. In the other examples, the oscillation is large because the periodic driving frequency matches a natural frequency of the system.

perOption.A: Correct. A stronger driving force alone explains the larger amplitude.
perOption.B: Sound at a natural frequency can drive large vibrations in the glass.
perOption.C: Blowing across the mouth excites a resonance of the air in the bottle.
perOption.D: At a particular rotation speed, the drum drives the machine at a natural frequency.

difficultyReason: Recognising resonance in familiar situations requires distinguishing driving frequency from driving force.
misconception: Confusing a stronger drive with resonance

explanation.body: The maximum speed is $v_{\max}=\omega x_0$, where the amplitude $x_0$ is the initial displacement $X$. Since $p=mv$ and both $m$ and $\omega$ stay fixed, the maximum momentum is proportional to $X$. Halving $X$ therefore halves the maximum momentum to $0.5p$.

perOption.A: Squares the amplitude ratio, which applies to energy.
perOption.C: Treats momentum as inversely proportional to amplitude.
perOption.D: Treats momentum as inversely proportional to amplitude squared.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder).
difficultyReason: The student must connect maximum SHM speed to momentum at fixed mass.
misconception: Assuming momentum scales with amplitude squared
transcription:
When a spring-mass system is displaced by an initial displacement $X$ and released, it moves in a simple harmonic motion with a maximum momentum of $p$.

The same spring-mass system is now displaced by an initial displacement of $0.5X$.

What is the new maximum momentum of its motion, in terms of $p$?

A $0.25p$; B $0.5p$; C $2p$; D $4p$

explanation.body: The wave period is $T=1/f=5\ \mathrm{s}$, so the ball completes $20/5=4$ cycles. In each cycle the ball travels four amplitudes, giving a total distance of $4(0.70\times4)=11.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the crest-to-trough distance in each cycle.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal trough-to-crest spacing as the distance the ball travels per cycle.
perOption.C: Correct. The ball travels four amplitudes per cycle.
perOption.D: Uses the wave speed $f\lambda$ times the elapsed time.

issues: Printed key letter C differs from batch keyAnswer A.
difficultyReason: The student combines the number of periods with the vertical distance per cycle.
misconception: Confusing motion of the medium with wave propagation
transcription:
A transverse water wave is moving along the surface of some water. This causes a ball to move vertically without moving horizontally as it floats upon the surface. At one instant, the ball is at the position shown.

[Not-to-scale diagram of a rightward-travelling wave with a ball on the left crest, a vertical distance of $0.70\ \mathrm{m}$ from the equilibrium line to a crest, and a horizontal distance of $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$ from a trough to the next crest.]

The wave has a frequency of $0.20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and an amplitude of $0.70\ \mathrm{m}$. The distance between a trough and an adjacent peak is $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$.

What is the distance travelled by the ball in a time of $20\ \mathrm{s}$?

A $5.6\ \mathrm{m}$; B $9.6\ \mathrm{m}$; C $11.2\ \mathrm{m}$; D $19.2\ \mathrm{m}$

explanation.body: At A the nearby molecules are displaced to the right, and at C they are displaced to the left. The molecule at B has zero displacement while its neighbours are displaced towards it, giving the highest pressure. At D the molecule also has zero displacement, but its neighbours are displaced away from it, giving the lowest pressure.

perOption.A: The molecule and its neighbours are displaced to the right, so A is not a rarefaction centre.
perOption.B: The neighbouring molecules are displaced towards B, giving maximum pressure.
perOption.C: The molecule and its neighbours are displaced to the left, so C is not a rarefaction centre.
perOption.D: Correct. Neighbouring molecules are displaced away from D.

issues: Printed key letter D differs from batch keyAnswer A.
difficultyReason: The student must use the displacements of neighbouring molecules to infer local pressure.
transcription:
A sound wave travels from left to right across a room. The variation with distance across the room of the displacement of the air molecules at one instant is shown. At which distance will the air pressure be lowest?

[Graph of displacement against distance from the left-hand end of the room. Positive displacement is to the right and negative displacement is to the left. The sinusoidal curve starts at zero and rises. A is below the first crest, B is at the falling zero crossing, C is below the trough and D is at the rising zero crossing. The curve then rises to a second crest and returns to zero.]

explanation.body: Q and R are adjacent antinodes, so $\lambda/2=6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $\lambda=12\ \mathrm{cm}$. The oscilloscope shows $1.5$ periods in five divisions, giving $T=(5\times20\times10^{-6})/1.5\ \mathrm{s}$. Hence $f=1/T=15\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}=15\ \mathrm{kHz}$.

perOption.A: Treats the spacing between adjacent antinodes as a full wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct. The frequency is 15 kHz and the wavelength is 12 cm.
perOption.C: Uses 2.5 divisions per period and treats adjacent antinodes as one wavelength apart.
perOption.D: Uses 2.5 divisions per period instead of five divisions for 1.5 periods.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder). The stated frequency and wavelength imply a sound speed of 1800 m/s, atypical for air in the illustrated setup. The trace and antinode spacing still give B.
difficultyReason: The student must distinguish spatial antinode spacing from the time interval shown on the oscilloscope.
misconception: Taking adjacent antinodes to be one wavelength apart
transcription:
Stationary sound waves are investigated using the apparatus shown.

[A loudspeaker faces a board. Microphone positions Q and R lie on the line between them, with R closer to the board. The microphone at R is connected to an oscilloscope.]

Q and R are adjacent positions of the microphone that give maximum amplitude on the oscilloscope, as shown.

[Oscilloscope screen when the microphone is at R. A sinusoidal trace spans about three periods across ten horizontal divisions on a grid six divisions high.]

The distance QR is $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and the time base of the oscilloscope is $20\ \mathrm{\mu s\,div^{-1}}$. What are the frequency and the wavelength of the sound wave?

Options (frequency in kHz, wavelength in cm)
A 15, 6.0
B 15, 12
C 20, 6.0
D 20, 12

explanation.body: For double-slit interference, the bright-fringe spacing is $x=\lambda D/a$. Thus $\lambda=xa/D=(8.0\times10^{-3})(0.1\times10^{-3})/2.0=4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$. The second dark fringe has path difference $1.5\lambda=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the path difference for the first dark fringe.
perOption.B: Uses one wavelength, the path difference for the first bright fringe.
perOption.C: Correct. The second dark fringe occurs at a path difference of $1.5\lambda$.
perOption.D: Uses two wavelengths, the path difference for the second bright fringe.

issues: Printed key letter C differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder).
difficultyReason: The student must calculate wavelength from fringe spacing and identify the second destructive-interference order.
misconception: Using an integer wavelength for a dark fringe
transcription:
Monochromatic light is incident on a pair of narrow slits a distance of $0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. A series of bright and dark fringes are observed on a screen a distance of $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ away. The distance between adjacent bright fringes is $8.0\ \mathrm{mm}$.

[Not-to-scale diagram showing monochromatic light incident from the left on the slits and a screen $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ to the right. The screen labels the central “zero” order bright fringe, the second order dark fringe above it, and an $8.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ spacing between adjacent bright fringes.]

What is the path difference between the light waves from the two slits that meet at the second order dark fringe?

A $2.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$
B $4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$
C $6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$
D $8.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$

explanation.body: Using the uniform-field model between the plates, $E=V/d$, where $d$ is the full separation. At P, $E=9.0/0.090=100\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides by the plate diameter instead of the plate separation.
perOption.B: Correct. The full plate separation is 0.090 m.
perOption.C: Divides the full potential difference by the distance from P to X.
perOption.D: Divides the full potential difference by the distance from P to Y.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder). The key assumes a uniform field. The finite plate diameter is only twice the separation, so fringing can limit the accuracy of this approximation.
difficultyReason: The calculation is direct once the full plate separation is identified.
misconception: Using the distance to one plate in the uniform-field formula
transcription:
Two parallel circular metal plates X and Y, each of diameter $18\ \mathrm{cm}$, have a separation of $9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. A potential difference of $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is applied between them.

[Plate X is above P and connected to the negative terminal. Plate Y is below P and connected to the positive terminal. Vertical arrows label the $9.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ plate separation, $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from X to P, and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from P to Y. The diameter of X is labelled $18\ \mathrm{cm}$.]

Point P is $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the surface of plate X and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the surface of plate Y.

What is the electric field strength at P?

A $50\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$; B $100\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$; C $150\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$; D $300\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

explanation.body: The electric field of a point charge obeys $E\propto 1/r^2$. If $E'$ is the field at $2r$, then $E/E'=(2r)^2/r^2=4$, so $E'=E/4$.

perOption.A: Correct. Doubling the distance reduces the field by a factor of four.
perOption.B: Uses an inverse-linear dependence on distance.
perOption.C: Assumes the field increases in direct proportion to distance.
perOption.D: Assumes the field increases with the square of distance.

difficultyReason: The student applies the inverse-square law to a doubled distance.

explanation.body: From $I=nAv_dq$, the drift speed is $v_d=I/(nAq)$. The cross-sectional area increases from X to Y and the current stays constant, so the drift speed decreases. Graphs B and D show an increase, while graph C would mean the electrons stop at Y.

perOption.A: Correct. The drift speed decreases and stays positive at Y.
perOption.B: Shows an increase in drift speed as the cross-sectional area increases.
perOption.C: Shows the drift speed dropping to zero at Y.
perOption.D: Shows a linear increase in drift speed from zero at X.

issues: The question PNG cuts off the option graphs, which were transcribed from key page 16. The working continues on page 17 and describes electrons moving from X to Y, although the cell polarity makes them drift from Y to X. The drift-speed profile and answer A are valid.
difficultyReason: The student must infer the curve from constant current and linearly increasing cross-sectional area.
misconception: Assuming drift speed falls linearly with area
transcription:
A wedge-shaped metal conductor of length $L$, varying width and uniform thickness is connected to a cell, as shown.

[The conductor widens linearly from X on the left to Y on the right. Its length is $L$. It is connected in a single loop to a cell with the positive terminal on the X side.]

Which graph best shows how the average drift velocity $v$ of electrons in the conductor varies with distance $x$ from end X?

[All four graphs plot $v$ against $x$ from 0 to $L$. A curves down from a positive value, flattening and staying above zero. B curves up from a positive value and flattens. C is a straight line dropping from a positive value to zero at $L$. D is a straight line increasing from zero at $x=0$.]

explanation.body: The voltmeter and resistor $R$ are in parallel, so both have a p.d. of $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$. This parallel combination is in series with Q across the $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$ supply, leaving $9.0-3.0=6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ across Q. If each parallel resistance is $R$, their effective resistance is $R/2$. The potential-divider ratio gives $(R/2)/R_Q=3/6$, so the voltmeter-to-Q resistance ratio is $R/R_Q=1$.

perOption.A: Ignores the voltmeter’s resistance when finding the equivalent resistance of the parallel branch.
perOption.B: Correct. The voltmeter and Q have equal resistance.
perOption.C: Uses the reciprocal voltage ratio as the requested resistance ratio without accounting for the parallel branch.
perOption.D: Inverts the branch-to-Q voltage ratio before converting from the equivalent resistance to the voltmeter resistance.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A.
difficultyReason: The student must include the voltmeter’s finite resistance when applying the potential-divider ratio.

explanation.body: By the right-hand grip rule, the fields add between the wires and oppose outside them. At the $40\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.10)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.20)}=\frac{12.5\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. At the $50\ \mathrm{cm}$ mark, $B=\frac{\mu_0(2I)}{2\pi(0.20)}+\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(0.10)}=\frac{10\mu_0 I}{\pi}$. The greatest resultant is at $40\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: The weaker wire’s field opposes the stronger wire’s field at 20 cm.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields reinforce and the stronger wire is closer.
perOption.C: The fields reinforce, but the nearer wire carries the smaller current.
perOption.D: The two fields oppose at 70 cm, where the closer wire carries the smaller current.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder).
difficultyReason: The student must find field directions and compare the sums at different distances from the two wires.
misconception: Adding field magnitudes where the fields oppose

explanation.body: The electric force on the electrons is upwards, so the magnetic force must act downwards to keep the beam undeflected. Conventional current is to the left. Fleming’s left-hand rule then gives a magnetic field into the paper.

perOption.A: Correct. The magnetic force is downwards.
perOption.B: An outward field gives an upward magnetic force that reinforces the electric force.
perOption.C: An upward field gives a magnetic force into the paper.
perOption.D: A downward field gives a magnetic force out of the paper.

difficultyReason: The student must reverse the electron motion to obtain conventional current before applying Fleming’s rule.
misconception: Using electron motion as conventional current
transcription:
A beam of electrons, travelling horizontally towards the right, passes between two horizontal charged parallel metal plates.

[The beam travels to the right midway between a positive upper plate and a negative lower plate.]

There is a vertical electric field between the plates. There is no deflection of the beam because of the presence of a uniform magnetic field in the region between the plates.

In which direction must this magnetic field be?

A into the paper
B out of the paper
C vertically upwards
D vertically downwards

explanation.body: The field component normal to the coil is $B\sin60^\circ$. Flipping the coil reverses the sign of the flux linkage, so the magnitude of the change is $NA[B\sin60^\circ-(-B\sin60^\circ)]$. Substituting gives $4(0.30)[0.045\sin60^\circ-(-0.045\sin60^\circ)]=0.094\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$.

perOption.A: Compares the magnitudes of the two linkages and misses the sign reversal.
perOption.B: $0.012\ \mathrm{Wb}$ is approximately the initial flux through one turn, before counting all four turns and the reversal.
perOption.C: Uses a change smaller than even the initial linkage magnitude of about $0.047\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The signed flux linkage reverses.

issues: Printed key letter D differs from batch keyAnswer A.
difficultyReason: The student must resolve the normal component of the field and account for the reversal of the area vector.
misconception: Ignoring the sign reversal of flux linkage
transcription:
A magnetic field of uniform flux density $0.045\ \mathrm{T}$ is at an angle of $60^\circ$ below the plane of horizontal coil of wire as shown.

[A horizontal circular coil is crossed by parallel magnetic field arrows pointing down and to the right. A dashed line in the coil’s plane makes a $60^\circ$ angle with the field lines.]

The coil of wire has 4 turns and cross sectional area of $0.30\ \mathrm{m^2}$.

What is the magnitude of the change in magnetic flux linkage of the coil of wire when it is flipped over $180^\circ$ about a horizontal axis?

A $0\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; B $0.012\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; C $0.035\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$; D $0.094\ \mathrm{Wb\,turns}$

explanation.body: Square the voltage and average it over one full $5.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ period, then take the square root. The zero-voltage interval contributes nothing, so $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4.0^2\times1.0+(-1.0)^2\times3.0)/5.0}=\sqrt{3.8}\ \mathrm{V}$. The mean power is $V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R=3.8/2.5=1.5\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: $0.98\ \mathrm{W}$ would require a mean-square voltage of $2.45\ \mathrm{V^2}$, but the $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ pulse alone contributes $3.2\ \mathrm{V^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct. Mean power is mean-square voltage divided by resistance.
perOption.C: Averages only over the four milliseconds with nonzero voltage.
perOption.D: $2.4\ \mathrm{W}$ would require a mean-square voltage of $6.0\ \mathrm{V^2}$, overestimating the contribution of the brief $4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ pulse.

issues: Printed key letter B differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder).
difficultyReason: The student must square each voltage level, weight it by its duration and convert the mean square to power.
misconception: Using mean voltage or a sinusoidal RMS formula for a stepped waveform
transcription:
The variation with time $t$ of the voltage $V$ of an alternating source applied across a $2.5\ \Omega$ resistor is shown below.

[Step graph of $V$ in volts against $t$ in milliseconds from 0 to 10.0. The voltage is 0 from 0 to 1.0 ms, $+4.0\ \mathrm{V}$ from 1.0 to 2.0 ms, and $-1.0\ \mathrm{V}$ from 2.0 to 5.0 ms. This pattern repeats from 5.0 to 10.0 ms.]

What is the mean power dissipated in the resistor?

A $0.98\ \mathrm{W}$; B $1.5\ \mathrm{W}$; C $1.9\ \mathrm{W}$; D $2.4\ \mathrm{W}$

explanation.body: The minimum wavelength $\lambda_1$ occurs when an electron transfers all the kinetic energy it gained across the accelerating voltage to one X-ray photon in a single collision with a target atom. Changing the voltage therefore shifts $\lambda_1$. The peak at $\lambda_2$ comes from a characteristic energy-level difference in the target atoms, so changing the target metal shifts $\lambda_2$.

perOption.A: Assigns the cutoff wavelength to the target metal as well as the accelerating voltage.
perOption.B: Swaps the controls for the cutoff and the characteristic peak.
perOption.C: Treats the characteristic peak wavelength as dependent on the accelerating voltage.
perOption.D: Correct. The target sets the characteristic line and the voltage sets the cutoff.

issues: Printed key letter D differs from batch keyAnswer A (parser placeholder).
difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the short-wavelength cutoff from the characteristic line on the same spectrum.
misconception: Attributing the cutoff and characteristic peaks to the same cause
transcription:
The graph below shows the variation of X-ray intensity with wavelength emitted from an X-ray tube.

[Intensity is plotted against wavelength. The continuous spectrum begins on the wavelength axis at $\lambda_1$, rises to a broad maximum, then falls. Two narrow peaks appear on the falling background. The first peak is marked $\lambda_2$ and the second is taller and at a longer wavelength.]

The target metal and the accelerating voltage are varied. Which wavelengths will be affected by the changes?

Options (changing the target metal, changing the accelerating voltage)
A $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_1$
B $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$
C $\lambda_2$, $\lambda_2$
D $\lambda_2$, $\lambda_1$
